``` **Why this works:** `rowspan="2"` makes the Region header span both header rows, and `colspan="2"` merges Q1/Q2 under a single "2025" group header with `scope="colgroup"` describing the whole merged column. Explain srcset with the sizes attribute — how does the browser actually pick the file it downloads?

```html ``` **Why this works:** Each candidate in `srcset` is described by its intrinsic width in pixels (`400w`), not by a zoom factor. The browser takes the value produced by `sizes` — here "100% of viewport under 600px wide, otherwise 50% of viewport" — computes the actual slot width in device pixels (slot × devicePixelRatio), then downloads the smallest candidate that is at least that large, with a margin for uncertainty. On a 390px-wide phone with DPR 3, the slot is 390 CSS px = 1170 device px, so `chart-1600.jpg` is fetched; on a 1440px desktop at DPR 1 the slot is 720px, so `chart-800.jpg` wins. The key insight is that `sizes` describes the *layout* width the image will occupy — get that wrong and you either ship too many bytes or render a blurry image.

What meta tags should every production page include for SEO?

```html
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Arion Hosting — Fast Managed WordPress for Small Teams</title>
  <meta name="description"
        content="Managed WordPress hosting with automatic backups, global CDN and 24/7 support. 30-day money-back guarantee.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://arionhost.example/plans">

  <meta name="robots" content="index, follow">
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">
</head>
```

**Why this works:** `charset` must come first because the parser needs the encoding before it can decode the rest of the document. The `viewport` meta enables responsive layout on mobile; without it, phones render at a virtual 980px width and scale down. `<title>` (~50–60 chars) is the single strongest on-page ranking element and the text shown in search results and tabs. `description` is not a direct ranking factor but is usually used as the search snippet, so it drives click-through. `rel="canonical"` consolidates duplicate URLs (query strings, tracking params) onto one authoritative address so link equity is not split. Keep `robots` as `index, follow` (or omit it — that is the default) and only restrict specific pages that genuinely must stay out of the index.

**Why this works:** Social platforms do not execute your JavaScript or read `<title>` for previews — their crawlers parse Open Graph (`og:`) meta tags server-side. `og:image` must be an absolute URL, and declaring `width`/`height` (1200×630 is the sweet spot) prevents cropped or rejected previews. `twitter:card="summary_large_image"` opts into the big-image layout on X/Twitter; Twitter falls back to the `og:` values when its own tags are missing, but explicit tags give you per-platform control of the copy. Because these crawlers rarely run JS, tags like these must be in the raw server-rendered HTML, not injected client-side.

Embed a YouTube video properly with an iframe — what attributes matter?

```html
<iframe
  src="https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ"
  title="Product launch keynote recording"
  width="560" height="315"
  loading="lazy"
  allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; picture-in-picture"
  allowfullscreen
  referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin">
</iframe>
```

**Why this works:** `title` is mandatory for accessibility — a screen reader announces it as the iframe's name; without it the frame is just an unnamed document. `loading="lazy"` defers loading the third-party frame (which pulls hundreds of KB) until it scrolls near the viewport, one of the cheapest performance wins available. The `youtube-nocookie.com` domain prevents tracking cookies from being set before playback. `allow` implements the Permissions Policy that gates powerful features like autoplay, and `allowfullscreen` is required because fullscreen is denied by default in cross-origin frames. Always size the frame explicitly — a width/height pair plus CSS `max-width: 100%` keeps the layout stable and avoids CLS.

Group related radio buttons and checkboxes with fieldset and legend. Why does this matter for accessibility?

```html
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Shipping speed</legend>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="shipping" value="standard" checked>
      Standard (3–5 days) — free
    </label>
    <label>
      <input type="radio" name="shipping" value="express">
      Express (1 day) — $12
    </label>
  </fieldset>

  <fieldset>
    <legend>Extras</legend>
    <label><input type="checkbox" name="gift"> Gift wrapping</label>
    <label><input type="checkbox" name="ins"> Insurance</label>
  </fieldset>

  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
```

**Why this works:** A `<fieldset>` groups its controls into one entity and its `<legend>` becomes the group's accessible name. When a screen reader lands on the third radio button it announces "Express (1 day), radio button, 2 of 2, Shipping speed" — without the legend, the user hears only "Express" with no context about what question is being answered. That context is also useful visually: the fieldset border frames the group. Note the shared `name="shipping"` is what makes the radios mutually exclusive (the browser inserts the group), while `checked` sets the default selection that gets submitted. Wrapping the input inside its `<label>` makes the whole row clickable without needing `for`/`id` pairing.

```html Arion — Documentation

Getting started

``` **Why this works:** The `lang` attribute on `` declares the document's primary language — screen readers pick the correct speech synthesis voice and pronunciation from it, and search engines use it for language targeting. Every inline switch of language must be re-declared (`lang="fa"` here) or the screen reader will read Persian text with an English voice, which is unintelligible. `dir="rtl"` on those elements flips text flow, punctuation, and embedding for the bidirectional algorithm. What are data-* attributes and when should I use them instead of classes or IDs?

``` **Why this works:** `data-*` is the standard extension point for embedding app data in markup: any attribute prefixed `data-` is guaranteed never to collide with future HTML features, is ignored by the browser's rendering, and is exposed on the JS side as camelCase keys in `element.dataset` (`data-price` → `dataset.price`). Classes should describe *what an element is* for styling, not carry machine state — mixing `data-stock="low"` into a class like `.low` couples your CSS to your data model. Explain exactly what defer and async do on a script tag, and which should I choose for analytics, a widget, and an app bundle?

```html
<head>
  <!-- App bundle: must run after DOM is parsed, in order -->
  <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>

  <!-- Independent analytics: fire whenever, never block -->
  <script src="https://cdn.example.com/analytics.js" async></script>

  <!-- Fallback: classic blocking script (avoid) -->
  <script src="/js/legacy.js"></script>
</head>
```

**Why this works:** A classic script pauses HTML parsing at the tag, downloads, executes, and only then resumes parsing — which is why legacy sites put scripts before `</body>`. `defer` downloads in parallel with parsing but guarantees two things: execution happens after the document is fully parsed, and multiple deferred scripts execute in document order. That makes `defer` the default choice for app bundles that query the DOM or depend on shared modules. `async` also downloads in parallel but executes the moment it arrives, in arrival order — ideal for analytics or third-party widgets that are self-contained and order-independent. Note `defer`/`async` are ignored on inline scripts, and `type="module"` is deferred by default, so a module script needs no attribute unless it must run even earlier.
